questions.subtopic: 1B1 Acting with integrity. Pressure to drop a finding
questions.question: A seafood plant manager asks internal auditor Marek to drop a significant finding on missed cold-storage checks from the draft, because repairs have started. Which response BEST shows honesty and professional courage?

options.A: Hold the draft until repairs finish, so no finding is needed
options.B: Cover the finding at the closing meeting, not in the draft
options.C: Keep the finding and acknowledge the repairs already under way
options.D: Keep the finding but lower its rating now that repairs have begun

questions.key_concept: A significant finding stays in the communication at its true significance; action management has started is acknowledged beside it, not traded for a softer result.
questions.pre_read: Separate two things: what the evidence showed, and what management has done about it since.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.1 Honesty and Professional Courage forbids hiding or leaving out a finding, and Standard 15.1 Final Engagement Communication has the internal auditor acknowledge action that management has already begun. So the finding stays, with the repairs noted beside it. Lowering the rating is the runner-up: significance rests on likelihood and impact under Standard 14.3 Evaluation of Findings, and repairs that have only started have not yet reduced either.

wrong_explanations.A: Waiting does not remove what the evidence showed. The condition existed, so it is reported as a finding and in time, with any started or finished action acknowledged.
wrong_explanations.B: Telling the manager aloud while leaving a significant finding out of the communication is still an omission; its other readers never learn of the risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the finding survives, but its rating follows likelihood and impact. Repairs that have only begun are acknowledged, not counted as a lower risk.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a condition that existed is still reported and in time, and B, because a significant finding left out of the communication is an omission.
Final two: C beats D because started repairs are acknowledged beside the finding; the rating changes when likelihood or impact has actually changed.
Exam cue: when management has started fixing a problem, CIA answers usually keep the finding at its true significance and acknowledge the action.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Acting with integrity. Following up a senior executive's breach
questions.question: An airport's chief audit executive told the board that the chief procurement officer took forbidden supplier gifts; three months on, internal auditor Oksana sees no response. Which step BEST matches the Standards' preferred practice?

options.A: Follow up and confirm that suitable action has been taken
options.B: Leave the response to the board, which now owns the decision
options.C: Report the gifts to the airport's regulator without further delay
options.D: Start an investigation into the officer's other supplier dealings

questions.key_concept: After an ethics concern about senior management reaches the board, internal auditors should follow up and confirm that suitable action was taken.
questions.pre_read: Reporting was one step. Ask what the Standards expect once the board has been told and nothing visible follows.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.2 Organization's Ethical Expectations requires concerns to be reported as policies and procedures direct. Its considerations add what should follow when the board or senior management is involved: internal auditors follow up and confirm that suitable action was taken. Leaving the response to the board is the runner-up: the decision is the board's, but the considerations do not end internal audit's part at the report.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the response is the board's to decide, but internal auditors should still follow up and confirm that suitable action was taken.
wrong_explanations.C: Reports outside the organization follow what laws, regulations and policies specify. Nothing here requires one, and the board already has the matter.
wrong_explanations.D: Reporting a concern does not make internal audit the investigator. Those with authority decide on any investigation; internal auditors confirm that action followed.

tips: Eliminate: C, because outside reports follow what law and policy specify, and D, because an investigation is for those with authority to decide, not a follow-up step.
Final two: A beats B because telling the board is not the last step; internal auditors should follow up and confirm that suitable action was taken.
Exam cue: for an ethics concern about senior management, expect two preferred practices: the chief audit executive tells the board, and internal auditors follow up. Both are shoulds.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Acting with integrity. Tolerated legal violation
questions.question: Internal auditor Kofi finds a gold refinery understating export weights; customs law obliges anyone who discovers this to notify the authority within 14 days, and executives tolerate the practice. What is Kofi's BEST course?

options.A: Tell the compliance officer and leave the rest to management
options.B: Notify the authority by day 14 if management does not stop it
options.C: Treat the practice as a risk that executives have accepted
options.D: Make sure the customs authority is notified within the 14 days

questions.key_concept: When a law requires a disclosure, the internal auditor makes sure it is made, on time, even if management tolerates the violation.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the law in the stem demands, of whom, and by when.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.3 Legal and Ethical Behavior requires internal auditors to obey the laws that apply to the organization, including making the disclosures those laws demand. Here the law itself names the authority and a deadline, so the outside report is the requirement, alongside any internal one. Notifying the authority if management fails to act is the runner-up, but the duty runs from discovery and does not depend on what management does.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal reporting is right as far as it goes, but the law places the duty on whoever discovers the declarations. It cannot be left to a management that tolerates them.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it keeps the authority in view, but the legal duty is not conditional on management's response, and the 14 days run from discovery.
wrong_explanations.C: Tolerance by executives does not lift the duties in Standard 1.3. Overlooking illegal activity the organization tolerates is itself discreditable conduct.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a duty the law places on the discoverer cannot be left to management, and C, because executive tolerance does not cancel the duty to act on a legal violation.
Final two: D beats B because the legal duty is unconditional and its deadline runs from discovery, whatever management then does.
Exam cue: when a law requires an outside report, it is made on time, through the function's route where time allows. Without such a law, the route policy sets applies.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. Objectivity or independence
questions.question: A courier's internal audit function reports directly to the board, yet a supervisor finds internal auditor Akinyi skipped required retesting at a depot run by a close friend. Which conclusion is MOST accurate?

options.A: The function's independence is impaired despite its reporting line
options.B: The auditor's objectivity is impaired despite the reporting line
options.C: The reporting line shows that the auditor's work was unbiased
options.D: A friendship without money involved creates no impairment

questions.key_concept: Independence belongs to the internal audit function and comes from its position; objectivity is each internal auditor's own unbiased mindset.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose problem this is: the function's place in the organization, or one person's judgment.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.1 Individual Objectivity requires each internal auditor to keep an impartial, unbiased mindset, and Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity requires them to avoid conflicts of interest, which a close friendship can create. The problem sits with one person's judgment. Calling it an independence impairment is the runner-up, but independence describes the function's position, which the direct reporting line to the board already supports.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: something is impaired, but independence is the function's freedom from conditions that bias its work. The board reporting line is intact; one auditor's judgment is not.
wrong_explanations.C: A sound reporting line supports objectivity but cannot supply it. Each internal auditor must still keep an unbiased mindset on every engagement.
wrong_explanations.D: Conflicts of interest include personal relationships and favoritism, not just financial ties. The test is whether judgment could be influenced, or appear to be.

tips: Eliminate: C, because board reporting supports objectivity but cannot prove one auditor is unbiased, and D, because relationships count as conflicts, with or without money.
Final two: B beats A because the bias sits in one auditor's judgment; independence is about the function's position, which is sound here.
Exam cue: function and reporting line point to independence; one person's bias, relationship or past role points to objectivity.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. Recent former responsibility
questions.question: Internal auditor Meera managed a lender's collections unit until seven months ago and disclosed this to the chief audit executive. Which assessment of Meera leading an assurance engagement on collections is MOST accurate?

options.A: Disclosing the former role has restored Meera's objectivity
options.B: Meera's objectivity is presumed impaired for this work
options.C: The function's independence is impaired by Meera's earlier transfer
options.D: Objectivity is unaffected now that Meera has left the unit

questions.key_concept: For assurance over an activity an internal auditor was responsible for in the past 12 months, objectivity is presumed impaired; disclosure does not lift that.
questions.pre_read: Check two facts first: is the engagement assurance or advisory, and how long ago did the responsibility end?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity tells internal auditors to refrain from assessing an activity they used to be responsible for, and for assurance work it presumes objectivity is impaired when that responsibility ended in the past 12 months. Seven months is inside the window. Relying on the disclosure is the runner-up, but disclosure to the requesting party is the condition for advisory work, not a cure for assurance.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: disclosure is required, and it is the condition for advisory work on a former responsibility. For assurance inside 12 months the presumption of impairment remains.
wrong_explanations.C: Independence concerns the function's position and reporting line. A past job held by one internal auditor is a question of that person's objectivity.
wrong_explanations.D: Leaving the unit does not remove the pull of judging one's own earlier decisions. The presumption runs for 12 months after the responsibility ended.

tips: Eliminate: C, because one auditor's past role is an objectivity matter, not the function's independence, and D, because the presumption lasts 12 months after the role ended.
Final two: B beats A because disclosure clears advisory work, not assurance; inside 12 months, objectivity is still presumed impaired.
Exam cue: former responsibility plus assurance plus under 12 months means presumed impaired. Look for the option that keeps that auditor off the assessment.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. Spotting a conflict of interest
questions.question: A chief audit executive is staffing an assurance engagement on this year's grant awards at a regional arts fund. Which internal auditor's circumstance MOST clearly creates a conflict of interest?

options.A: Sits with the grants manager on the staff social committee
options.B: Donates yearly to a museum that is not an applicant
options.C: Won a grant from the fund six years ago, before being hired
options.D: Serves as an unpaid board member of a current applicant

questions.key_concept: A conflict of interest is a competing personal or professional interest; an unpaid role with a party the engagement affects counts, in fact or appearance.
questions.pre_read: For each circumstance, ask what the auditor personally stands to gain, lose or protect from the engagement's results.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity requires internal auditors to avoid conflicts of interest: a competing personal or professional interest that could sway judgment, or appear to. A board seat with a current applicant gives the auditor a stake in who wins grants, paid or not. The old grant is the runner-up: it is a real link to the fund, but it closed years ago and leaves nothing to gain or lose from this year's awards.

wrong_explanations.A: A staff committee is ordinary working contact, not a close personal relationship, and it gives the auditor no stake in who wins grants.
wrong_explanations.B: A donation is a financial tie, but to a body with no application before the fund. Nothing in the awards can help or harm that interest.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a past grant is a link to the fund, but it closed six years ago. The auditor has nothing to gain or lose from this year's awards.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a shared staff committee is ordinary working contact with no stake in the awards, and B, because a donation to a non-applicant leaves no interest in them.
Final two: D beats C because a board seat with a current applicant is a live interest in this year's awards; a grant won six years ago is not.
Exam cue: a conflict of interest needs a competing interest, such as a role, relationship or investment tied to the outcome. Money is not required.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. Familiarity bias in testing
questions.question: After four clean audits of the same branch, internal auditor Thandi halves the sample and accepts the manager's explanation for two anomalies without checking. What is the GREATEST risk to the engagement?

options.A: Conclusions rest on past impressions instead of current evidence
options.B: The function loses its organizational independence from the branch
options.C: Objectivity is presumed impaired after four audits there
options.D: A conflict of interest arises between Thandi and the manager

questions.key_concept: Familiarity bias lets assumptions from past experience stand in for evidence, which weakens professional skepticism and the support for conclusions.
questions.pre_read: Look at what changed in the auditor's testing, and what that change was based on.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.1 Individual Objectivity requires internal auditors to be aware of their biases and manage them, and its considerations give familiarity bias as an example: assumptions from past experience that weaken professional skepticism. Thandi's smaller sample and unchecked explanations mean this year's conclusions lean on earlier years. A conflict of interest is the runner-up, but nothing shows a competing personal interest; the threat is assumption, not a stake.

wrong_explanations.B: Independence is the function's position, set by its reporting line to the board. One auditor's habits on one branch are a matter of personal objectivity.
wrong_explanations.C: The presumption in Standard 2.2 concerns assurance over a recent former responsibility. The Standards set no limit on auditing one unit again; rotation is a may.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: long contact can strain objectivity, but a conflict of interest needs a competing interest or close tie. The facts show assumptions from clean results instead.

tips: Eliminate: B, because independence concerns the function's position, not one auditor's habits, and C, because the Standards presume impairment after a former responsibility, not after repeat audits.
Final two: A beats D because nothing shows a competing interest; the danger is past clean results replacing evidence gathered this year.
Exam cue: repeated clean audits followed by lighter testing signal familiarity bias. On CIA questions the harm is weaker skepticism and thinly supported conclusions.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Policies and safeguards for objectivity. Gift during an engagement
questions.question: Midway through an audit of a stadium's ticketing, the ticketing manager offers internal auditor Yusuf two match seats worth less than the organization's gift limit. Which consideration matters MOST in deciding whether Yusuf may accept?

options.A: Whether the seats' value is under the organization's gift limit
options.B: Whether the seats count as a gift or as mere hospitality
options.C: Whether accepting could be presumed to impair Yusuf's objectivity
options.D: Whether accepting would in fact bias Yusuf's audit conclusions

questions.key_concept: A gift or favor is refused whenever it may impair objectivity or look as if it does; actual bias and value limits do not decide.
questions.pre_read: Notice who is offering, when, and what the organization's limit does and does not tell you.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity bars internal auditors from accepting any item, tangible or not, that may impair objectivity or be presumed to. Seats offered by the manager of the activity under review, during the engagement, meet that test whatever they cost. Whether Yusuf's conclusions would really change is the runner-up, but the rule does not wait for actual bias: how acceptance could reasonably look to others is enough.

wrong_explanations.A: The organization's limit is a ceiling for staff in general. The test for an internal auditor is whether objectivity may be impaired, or be presumed to be.
wrong_explanations.B: The rule covers any item, tangible or intangible, so hospitality and favors count as much as objects or cash. The label put on the seats does not decide it.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: actual bias would certainly matter, but the test is wider. An item is refused when others could presume it sways the auditor, even if Yusuf stays fair.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the organization's limit does not answer the objectivity test, and B, because hospitality and favors are covered as much as tangible gifts.
Final two: C beats D because the rule turns on presumed impairment, in appearance as well as in fact; Yusuf's own fairness does not settle it.
Exam cue: for gifts, ask how acceptance would look to an outsider. On CIA questions, value limits and good intentions rarely rescue a gift from the manager of the activity under review.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Policies and safeguards for objectivity. Assurance over an area the chief audit executive runs
questions.question: A shipyard's chief audit executive also heads business continuity, an ongoing role the charter records, and an assurance engagement on business continuity is planned. Which arrangement BEST protects the engagement's objectivity?

options.A: A senior audit manager oversees it and reports to the board
options.B: The chief audit executive oversees it after informing the board
options.C: The auditors assigned sign statements confirming their own objectivity
options.D: An independent overseer from outside internal audit is engaged

questions.key_concept: If the area under review belongs to the chief audit executive, nobody inside internal audit can oversee its assurance; the overseer comes from outside.
questions.pre_read: Trace the reporting line of each person proposed to oversee the work. Where does it end?
questions.correct_explanation: Everyone in internal audit answers to the chief audit executive. So when that executive also runs the area being assured, Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity hands oversight of the engagement to someone independent who is not part of the function, and Standard 7.1 Organizational Independence wants assurance over such a role obtained another way. A senior audit manager reporting to the board is the runner-up, but that manager still works for the impaired executive.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: reporting this one engagement to the board helps, but the manager is still inside the function and answers to the impaired executive. Oversight must come from outside.
wrong_explanations.B: Telling the board is required, but disclosure does not remove the impairment. The executive would still be overseeing an assessment of their own function.
wrong_explanations.C: Signed statements deal with each auditor's personal impairments. The problem sits above them: everyone assigned still answers to the executive who runs the area.

tips: Eliminate: B, because disclosure to the board does not remove the executive's impairment, and C, because personal statements do not change who the auditors answer to.
Final two: D beats A because everyone inside internal audit answers to the chief audit executive; a party outside the function is free of that tie.
Exam cue: when the chief audit executive runs the area under review, look for oversight from outside internal audit, not a more senior insider.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Policies and safeguards for objectivity. Impairment found after the engagement
questions.question: Two months after an engagement on an outsourced payroll provider closed, a chief audit executive learns the lead auditor held shares in the provider, though no error has surfaced. What should the executive do FIRST?

options.A: Disclose the concern to the stakeholders the results affect
options.B: Note it in the next annual independence confirmation to the board
options.C: Have another auditor repeat the work before raising the matter
options.D: Leave the results in place unless an actual error is found

questions.key_concept: An impairment found after an engagement, in fact or appearance, is first taken up with those affected; the chief audit executive then decides the action.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether reliability has to be damaged in fact, or whether looking damaged is enough to act.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.3 Disclosing Impairments to Objectivity covers an impairment discovered after completion that puts the results' reliability in doubt, in fact or in appearance. It falls to the chief audit executive to take the matter up with the parties affected and then decide what follows. Perception alone triggers the duty. Repeating the work first is the runner-up; re-performance may be the agreed action, but it comes after disclosure, not in place of it.

wrong_explanations.B: The yearly confirmation covers the function's independence. One auditor's impairment that puts issued results in doubt is discussed with those affected now, not at year end.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: repeating the work may be the right remedy, but the chief audit executive first discusses the concern with those affected, then determines the action.
wrong_explanations.D: The duty covers perceived reliability as well as actual. Results lose value when users doubt the auditor's objectivity, even with no error found.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the annual confirmation is about the function's independence and comes too late, and D, because perceived reliability counts even with no error found.
Final two: A beats C because disclosure and discussion with those affected come first; repeating the work may follow as the action determined.
Exam cue: an impairment discovered late still has to be disclosed. On CIA questions, discuss with the affected parties before choosing or starting the fix.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. Missing technical competency
questions.question: Internal auditor Ines is assigned to lead an assurance engagement on a hospital's radiation-dosing software, a technology nobody in the function understands. What should Ines do FIRST?

options.A: Decline the engagement and ask to remove it from the plan
options.B: Begin fieldwork and build the needed knowledge while testing proceeds
options.C: Discuss the missing competency with the chief audit executive
options.D: Narrow the scope to the parts the team already understands

questions.key_concept: Internal auditors take on work they have or can obtain the competencies for; a resource gap found in planning goes to the chief audit executive.
questions.pre_read: Before choosing, ask whether a missing skill can be brought in, and who has the means to arrange that.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 3.1 Competency lets internal auditors take on work they can attain the competencies for, and Standard 13.5 Engagement Resources has them raise inappropriate or insufficient resources with the chief audit executive, who can obtain the expertise through training, a guest auditor or an outside provider. Narrowing the scope is the runner-up: it may follow if expertise cannot be found, but it is not the first move.

wrong_explanations.A: A missing skill is not a reason to drop planned work. The competency can be obtained, for example through a specialist, training or an external provider.
wrong_explanations.B: Learning on the job works under a supervisor who has the competency. Nobody in the function has it, so the tests would be designed and run without it.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a reduced scope can result when expertise cannot be obtained, but that comes after the discussion with the chief audit executive, not before it.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a missing competency can be obtained and need not end the engagement, and B, because self-teaching during fieldwork leaves the testing without the competency it needs.
Final two: C beats D because the first duty is to raise the resource gap so expertise can be obtained; cutting scope is a later fallback.
Exam cue: when the team lacks a skill, CIA answers usually obtain it, through the chief audit executive, before they decline, improvise or shrink the work.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. Keeping competencies current
questions.question: Internal auditor Rahim, certified for ten years, audits treasury at a bank that is moving to a real-time payments platform Rahim has never reviewed. Which response BEST meets Rahim's professional development duty?

options.A: Complete the certification's required hours on familiar treasury topics
options.B: Arrange training on the platform before the engagement begins
options.C: Ask the chief audit executive to assign the engagement to another auditor
options.D: Add the platform to next year's personal development plan

questions.key_concept: Keeping competencies current for the work at hand is each internal auditor's own responsibility; certification hours alone do not close a specific gap.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the development duty is for, and who has to act on it.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 3.2 Continuing Professional Development requires internal auditors to keep developing their competencies so their services stay effective, and Standard 3.1 Competency makes each auditor responsible for the competencies their own work needs. A platform Rahim has never reviewed is the gap. Completing the certification's hours on familiar topics is the runner-up: certified auditors must meet those rules too, but hours that miss the gap leave the competency unbuilt.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: meeting the certification's education rules is also required, but the duty is to develop the competencies the work needs. Familiar topics leave the platform gap open.
wrong_explanations.C: Standard 3.1 lets internal auditors take on work they can become competent for. Stepping aside leaves the gap in place; the development duty is to close it.
wrong_explanations.D: A plan for next year comes after the engagement. The need exists now, and development is meant to keep services effective as the work changes.

tips: Eliminate: C, because stepping aside leaves a gap that can be closed in time, and D, because a development goal for next year comes after the engagement.
Final two: B beats A because development must build the competencies the work needs; certification hours on familiar topics meet a separate rule and leave the gap.
Exam cue: a new system, law or role signals a development need. On CIA questions the auditor acts on that specific gap personally and early.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. Disagreement at the closing meeting
questions.question: At a closing meeting, a wine exporter's logistics head disputes a finding on customs paperwork but offers no new facts or reasoning, and discussion brings no agreement. What is the internal auditor's BEST next step?

options.A: Keep the finding and let both sides put their positions on record
options.B: Keep the finding and treat the unsupported objection as settled
options.C: Lower the finding's rating until both sides accept it
options.D: Take the dispute straight to the board for a decision

questions.key_concept: When management disagrees, internal auditors seek mutual understanding; without a valid reason the results stand, and both positions are recorded as the methodology provides.
questions.pre_read: Check what the manager brought to the meeting: new facts, or disagreement alone?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.1 Engagement Communication has internal auditors discuss a disagreement and try for a mutual understanding. If none is reached, they need not change the results without a valid reason, and they follow the methodology that lets both sides state their positions. Treating the objection as settled is the runner-up: the finding rightly stands, but even a weak objection gets its place on record, which the methodology exists to provide.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the finding rightly stands, but Standard 13.1 has internal auditors follow the methodology that lets both sides set out their positions, however weak the objection.
wrong_explanations.C: Results change for a valid reason such as new facts or a sound argument. Significance is rated on likelihood and impact, not negotiated to win agreement.
wrong_explanations.D: The board is not the first stop for a disputed finding. Both positions go on record, and the chief audit executive should then seek a resolution with senior management.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a rating changes for a valid reason, not to win agreement, and D, because a disputed finding is documented and worked through with senior management before any board involvement.
Final two: A beats B because both keep the finding, but the methodology gives management's position a place on record even when it brings no new facts.
Exam cue: in a disagreement with no new facts or sound argument, CIA answers keep the results and record both views, not one.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Due professional care and skepticism. Cost against benefit
questions.question: A new internal auditor at a tram operator says due professional care means the budget should not limit testing. Which reply from the engagement supervisor is MOST accurate?

options.A: Care means testing until no significant error could remain undetected
options.B: Care governs how tests are done; the budget belongs to planning
options.C: Care lets cost set the scope whenever hours are tight
options.D: Care includes weighing the work's cost against its likely benefit

questions.key_concept: Due professional care includes weighing the cost of the work against its potential benefit; it is not a duty to test everything.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether care is about the amount of testing or about the judgment behind it.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 4.2 Due Professional Care lists the cost of the work against its potential benefits among the things an internal auditor must assess, next to the significance of risks and how probable significant errors, fraud and noncompliance are. So budget is weighed, not waved away. Letting cost set the scope is the runner-up, but cost is one factor balanced against benefit and risk, not the deciding one.

wrong_explanations.A: Nobody expects an internal auditor to be infallible. Care is the diligence and judgment of a prudent, competent auditor, not a promise that nothing is missed.
wrong_explanations.B: Due professional care applies to planning as well as performing. Deciding how much work is needed, and with which techniques, is part of exercising it.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: cost does count, but it is weighed against likely benefit and the significance of risks. Tight hours do not justify leaving a significant risk untested.

tips: Eliminate: A, because care is not infallibility or exhaustive testing, and B, because care covers planning as well as performing the work.
Final two: D beats C because cost is weighed against benefit and risk; it informs how much work is worth doing but does not decide alone.
Exam cue: due professional care means proportion. Be wary of options that test everything, and of options that let budget override significant risk.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Due professional care and skepticism. Care is not infallibility
questions.question: A regulator fines a credit union over an error in a process its internal auditors reviewed last year. Which question BEST tests whether the internal auditors exercised due professional care?

options.A: Did they examine every transaction in the reviewed process?
options.B: Did they work as a prudent, competent auditor would?
options.C: Did any significant error in the process go undetected?
options.D: Did the process managers agree with the engagement's results?

questions.key_concept: Due professional care is judged by whether the work matched what a prudent, competent internal auditor would do, not by whether every error was caught.
questions.pre_read: Decide whether care is measured by the outcome or by the quality of the planning and the work.
questions.correct_explanation: Principle 4 Exercise Due Professional Care describes care as the skepticism, judgment and diligence of a prudent, competent internal auditor, and adds that infallibility is not expected. So the test is how the work was planned and performed, including how risks were weighed under Standard 4.2. Asking whether an error slipped through is the runner-up, but it judges the outcome, and a careful engagement can still miss something.

wrong_explanations.A: Care weighs cost against benefit and the significance of risks. Examining every transaction is not required, and it would take resources from higher risks.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a missed error invites the question, but infallibility is not the standard. Care is judged by the work done, not by the outcome.
wrong_explanations.D: Management's agreement shows acceptance, not quality. Care is measured against a prudent, competent internal auditor's planning and performance.

tips: Eliminate: A, because care does not require testing every transaction, and D, because management's agreement does not measure the quality of the work.
Final two: B beats C because care is judged by how the work was planned and performed; a missed error alone does not prove a lack of care.
Exam cue: after a surprise loss or fine, CIA answers judge due professional care by process and judgment, not by hindsight.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Due professional care and skepticism. Corroborating a statement
questions.question: An IT manager at a veterinary group tells internal auditor Sofia that backups are restore-tested every month and offers a summary slide as support. Which response BEST shows professional skepticism?

options.A: Read the backup policy requiring a monthly restore test
options.B: Accept the statement and the slide as sufficient support
options.C: Inspect the restore-test logs for a sample of recent months
options.D: Ask the manager's team to confirm the tests in a signed memo

questions.key_concept: Professional skepticism tests whether information is reliable by seeking corroborating evidence, without assuming the person is right or dishonest.
questions.pre_read: For each response, ask where the supporting information would come from.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 4.3 Professional Skepticism requires internal auditors to assess critically how reliable information is and to seek more evidence where a statement may be incomplete. Standard 14.1 Gathering Information for Analyses and Evaluation adds that information is more reliable when the auditor obtains it directly or corroborates it. Inspecting the logs does that. A memo from the manager's team is the runner-up, but it is the same assertion from the same unit.

wrong_explanations.A: The policy shows what should happen, not what did. It is the criterion for the test; evidence of the restores themselves is still needed.
wrong_explanations.B: The statement and the slide come from the same manager, so nothing corroborates either. Skepticism means validating claims with evidence, not taking them on trust.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a second voice sounds like corroboration, but the manager's own team repeats the same assertion. Reliable evidence is obtained directly or from an independent source.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a policy is the criterion, not evidence that restores were tested, and B, because a statement and a slide from the same manager corroborate nothing.
Final two: C beats D because logs the auditor inspects are direct evidence; a memo from the manager's team repeats the assertion from the same unit.
Exam cue: ask what each piece of evidence actually shows and who produced it. CIA answers favor evidence the auditor obtains directly.

questions.subtopic: 1B6 Confidentiality and proper use of information. Ownership of workpapers
questions.question: Internal auditor Tane is leaving a dental chain and wants to keep copies of engagement workpapers as samples for job interviews. What is the BEST course of action?

options.A: Keep copies of the workpapers that Tane personally prepared
options.B: Keep copies after removing names and account numbers
options.C: Ask the management of each activity reviewed to approve the copies
options.D: Leave every copy in the internal audit function's custody

questions.key_concept: Engagement information stays the organization's; an internal auditor uses it for professional purposes and leaves records in the function's custody.
questions.pre_read: Ask who owns the information in a workpaper, and what purpose the planned use would serve.
questions.correct_explanation: Principle 5 Maintain Confidentiality has internal auditors use information for professional purposes and respect who owns it, and Standard 5.1 Use of Information bars using it for personal gain. Showing workpapers to a prospective employer would also disclose them to an unauthorized outside party, which Standard 5.2 Protection of Information forbids. Removing names is the runner-up: it eases the privacy concern, but the records are still the organization's and the use is still personal.

wrong_explanations.A: Preparing a workpaper does not make the auditor its owner. The information was obtained for the organization's audit work and remains the organization's.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: removing names protects individuals, but the content is still proprietary and the purpose is still personal benefit, not professional use.
wrong_explanations.C: The management of an activity under review does not control engagement records. Custody, retention and release follow the internal audit function's methodologies.

tips: Eliminate: A, because writing a workpaper does not transfer ownership to the auditor, and C, because the management of an activity under review does not control the function's records.
Final two: D beats B because redaction addresses privacy alone; ownership and the bar on personal use still apply to what remains.
Exam cue: access is not ownership. On CIA questions, engagement information serves the engagement and stays under the function's custody rules.

questions.subtopic: 1B6 Confidentiality and proper use of information. Privacy rules and audit access
questions.question: Citing the charter's unrestricted access, internal auditor Greta wants to copy patients' billing data to a personal analytics tool, though policy keeps personal data on secured servers with simpler tools. Which action is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Copy the data, relying on the charter's unrestricted access
options.B: Analyze the data on the secured servers with the tools provided
options.C: Copy the data to the personal tool with names removed
options.D: Have the billing team run the analysis and send the results

questions.key_concept: Unrestricted access lets internal auditors obtain information; laws, regulations and policies still govern how they use, move and store it.
questions.pre_read: Separate two questions: may the auditor see the data, and how must the data be handled once seen?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 5.1 Use of Information requires internal auditors to use information as the applicable rules direct: the law, regulations and the organization's own policies. Standard 5.2 Protection of Information adds those on privacy and information security. The charter grants access; it does not waive the handling rules. Removing names is the runner-up: it lowers the exposure, but the data would still leave the secured servers that the policy requires.

wrong_explanations.A: Access under the charter answers whether the auditor may see the data. Handling it is still governed by privacy law and the organization's policies.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: masking names reduces exposure, but billing records can still identify people, and the data would still leave the servers the policy requires.
wrong_explanations.D: The policy does not stop the auditor's own analysis; it fixes where the data stays. Results the billing team prepares are less reliable than work the auditor performs directly.

tips: Eliminate: A, because access under the charter does not waive privacy and handling rules, and D, because the auditor can still analyze the data directly, which is more reliable.
Final two: B beats C because the policy keeps personal data on the secured servers; stripping names lowers the risk but still moves the data off them.
Exam cue: the mandate gives access; law and policy govern use. On CIA questions the auditor does the work inside the handling rules.

questions.subtopic: 1B6 Confidentiality and proper use of information. Request from a senior colleague
questions.question: After an engagement on a plant closure plan restricted to a named project team, internal auditor Bashir is asked by a sales director outside that team which plant will close. Which response is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Decline, and explain that the plan is limited to authorized people
options.B: Decline, and state that the engagement did not cover plant closures
options.C: Answer verbally and keep the written workpapers restricted
options.D: Answer once the director promises to keep it confidential

questions.key_concept: Confidential information goes to people authorized to receive it, and a refusal to share it must still be truthful.
questions.pre_read: Two duties meet here. Check each response against both of them.
questions.correct_explanation: Principle 5 Maintain Confidentiality protects information from unauthorized disclosure inside the organization as well as outside, and Standard 5.2 Protection of Information bars disclosure to unauthorized parties unless a legal or professional responsibility applies. The director is outside the team the plan is restricted to, so Bashir declines. Declining with a cover story is the runner-up: it protects the plan, but Standard 1.1 Honesty and Professional Courage forbids a false statement.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it protects the plan, but with a false statement. Standard 1.1 requires internal auditors to be truthful, so the refusal has to be an honest one.
wrong_explanations.C: The duty covers information passed on in conversation as well as in documents. Telling the director aloud is still an unauthorized disclosure.
wrong_explanations.D: A promise limits further spread, but authorization comes from the organization's rules, not from the requester's rank or assurances.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a spoken answer is still an unauthorized disclosure, and D, because a promise of secrecy does not make the director authorized.
Final two: A beats B because both keep the plan confidential, but a refusal must be truthful; denying that the engagement covered closures is a false statement.
Exam cue: for any request for engagement information, ask one question first: is this person authorized to have it? Employment and seniority do not answer it.

questions.subtopic: 1B6 Confidentiality and proper use of information. Lawful demand for workpapers
questions.question: A court order addressed to internal auditor Dao requires a mine's safety workpapers within five days; the function's methodology has the chief audit executive authorize outside releases. What should Dao do FIRST?

options.A: Decline, treating the workpapers as confidential engagement records
options.B: Send the workpapers to the court personally before the deadline
options.C: Hand the order to the chief audit executive without any delay
options.D: Send the final communication and hold the workpapers back

questions.key_concept: A legal duty to disclose overrides confidentiality, but the release still follows the function's methodology, here through the chief audit executive.
questions.pre_read: Two questions are mixed here: whether the records may be released, and who handles the release.
questions.correct_explanation: A lawful order is a legal responsibility, so Standard 5.2 Protection of Information allows the disclosure and Standard 1.3 Legal and Ethical Behavior requires it. Who releases the records is a separate question. Standard 5.2 has internal auditors follow the procedures that apply, and the considerations of Standard 9.3 Methodologies list releasing records among the methodologies a function documents. Here that route runs through the chief audit executive, and five days allow it.

wrong_explanations.A: Confidentiality gives way to a legal responsibility to disclose, and internal auditors must make the disclosures the law requires. Refusing a lawful order is not an option.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the order must be met, but five days allow the function's route: the chief audit executive authorizes outside releases and can seek legal advice first.
wrong_explanations.D: A partial answer does not meet the order, and choosing what to hold back is not the auditor's call. Under the methodology the chief audit executive authorizes the release.

tips: Eliminate: A, because confidentiality yields to a legal duty to disclose, and D, because a partial release neither meets the order nor is the auditor's decision.
Final two: C beats B because both honor the order, but the methodology has the chief audit executive authorize outside releases, and five days leave time for it.
Exam cue: on outside requests for audit records, CIA answers neither refuse a lawful demand nor release alone. They follow the function's methodology for releases.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. Advice on a former responsibility
questions.question: Internal auditor Ravi ran a brewery's maintenance planning until four months ago; the chief audit executive, aware of this, wants Ravi to take the planning manager's request for scheduling advice. What must Ravi do FIRST?

options.A: Disclose the possible impairment to the manager who requested the advice
options.B: Decline the work while objectivity is presumed to be impaired
options.C: Have the chief audit executive confirm the advice cannot impair objectivity
options.D: Disclose the possible impairment to a designated supervisor in internal audit

questions.key_concept: Advisory work on a former responsibility is allowed once the possible impairment is disclosed to the requesting party; the 12-month presumption concerns assurance.
questions.pre_read: Check two things before the options: is the service advice or assurance, and who already knows about the past role?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity treats advice differently from assurance. An internal auditor may advise on an activity they once ran, as long as the party asking for the advice hears about the possible impairment before the engagement is accepted. The chief audit executive already knows, so that disclosure is the step left. Declining is the runner-up, but the presumption of impairment inside 12 months belongs to assurance work.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the presumption of impairment covers assurance within 12 months of the role. For advice, the work may go ahead once the requesting party has been told.
wrong_explanations.C: That confirmation is the rule for assurance that follows earlier advisory work. Here the service is advice, and the chief audit executive already knows the history.
wrong_explanations.D: Disclosure inside the function goes to the chief audit executive or a designated supervisor. The chief audit executive already knows; the requesting manager does not.

tips: Eliminate: C, because that confirmation is the rule for assurance after earlier advice, and D, because the chief audit executive already knows, so disclosure inside the function is done.
Final two: A beats B because the service is advice: the 12-month presumption covers assurance, and advice is allowed after disclosure to whoever asked.
Exam cue: a recent former responsibility plus assurance means presumed impaired; the same history plus advice means disclose to the requesting party, then proceed.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. An unbiased auditor in an impaired function
questions.question: Internal auditor Noor, with no ties to a port's finance unit, refused to drop two supported finance findings; the finance director, the chief audit executive's only reporting line, removed them. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: Both Noor's objectivity and the function's independence have been impaired
options.B: Noor's objectivity is impaired, and the function's independence is intact
options.C: Neither Noor's objectivity nor the function's independence is impaired
options.D: Noor's objectivity is intact, and the function's independence is impaired

questions.key_concept: Independence is the function's freedom from interference and comes from its reporting line; objectivity is one auditor's mindset. Either can fail while the other holds.
questions.pre_read: Take the two halves separately: did Noor's own judgment bend, and can the function report without interference?
questions.correct_explanation: Independence belongs to the function. Principle 7 Positioned Independently ties it to the chief audit executive reporting directly to the board, and the considerations of Standard 7.1 Organizational Independence name pressure to suppress findings as a threat. Here the only line runs to the finance director, who removed the findings. Objectivity is Noor's mindset, and the refusal shows it held. 'Both impaired' is the runner-up, but an overruled auditor is not a biased one.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the independence half is right. Objectivity, though, is Noor's own mindset: Noor judged on the evidence and refused to drop the findings, so that judgment held.
wrong_explanations.B: This fits the case where one auditor has a tie or a bias and the reporting line is sound. Here Noor is unbiased, and the reporting line is the weakness.
wrong_explanations.C: With no direct line to the board, a manager could strike findings on that manager's own area. That is interference with communicating results, which impairs the function.

tips: Eliminate: B, because Noor has no tie or bias and the reporting line is the weakness, and C, because findings removed by the audited area's director show interference.
Final two: D beats A because objectivity is Noor's mindset, and Noor refused to give way; being overruled by the finance director is a failure of the function's position.
Exam cue: judge the person and the function separately. Bias, ties and past roles are objectivity; reporting lines, restricted access and suppressed results are independence.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. When a job prospect becomes a conflict
questions.question: A senior logistics post opens while internal auditor Tomás is auditing logistics. At which point does a conflict of interest FIRST arise for Tomás?

options.A: When the logistics head announces the vacancy at a meeting Tomás attends
options.B: When the head invites Tomás to apply and Tomás wants the post
options.C: When Tomás submits an application and the head acknowledges it
options.D: When the head offers Tomás the post and Tomás accepts it

questions.key_concept: A conflict of interest exists once a personal interest may influence judgment, or appear to; it does not wait for a formal step.
questions.pre_read: Look for the earliest point at which Tomás has something personal to gain from the unit under review.
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards' glossary describes a conflict of interest as a situation that may influence an internal auditor's objective judgment, or appear to, and Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity counts potential and perceived impairments beside actual ones. Once the head of the unit under review invites Tomás and Tomás wants the post, a personal interest competes with the audit. A formal application is the runner-up, but it only records an interest that already exists.

wrong_explanations.A: Hearing an announcement made to everyone is not yet an interest: nothing here says Tomás wants the post or has been approached, so nothing could sway the work.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: applying makes the interest formal, but the conflict began earlier. A wanted post the audited unit's head invites Tomás to seek may already influence judgment, or appear to.
wrong_explanations.D: By an accepted offer the conflict is beyond doubt, and it has existed for some time. Impairments count when potential or perceived, not just when certain.

tips: Eliminate: A, because an announcement made to everyone gives no personal interest yet, and D, because by an accepted offer the conflict is long established.
Final two: B beats C because a wanted invitation from the audited unit's head can already sway judgment or seem to; applying merely makes it formal.
Exam cue: on timing questions about conflicts, pick the earliest point where an interest could influence the auditor or look as if it does. Disclosure to a supervisor follows at once.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. A former role in a different activity
questions.question: Internal auditor Mihi ran a hospital's patient billing team until six months ago and had no part in pharmacy purchasing. Which assessment of assigning Mihi to assurance work on pharmacy purchasing is MOST accurate?

options.A: Presumed impaired: the twelve-month presumption follows Mihi to any engagement
options.B: Presumed impaired until pharmacy management is told of the billing role
options.C: Assignable for advice on purchasing, though not for assurance
options.D: Assignable: the twelve-month presumption covers billing, which Mihi ran

questions.key_concept: The refrain rule and the 12-month presumption attach to the specific activity an internal auditor was responsible for, not to every area of the organization.
questions.pre_read: Compare two things: the activity Mihi used to be responsible for and the activity this engagement reviews.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity ties both the refrain rule and the 12-month presumption to the specific activity an internal auditor was responsible for. Mihi was responsible for patient billing, not pharmacy purchasing, so neither rule reaches this engagement and no special disclosure is triggered. A presumption that follows the auditor is the runner-up: the six months are real, but they count against assurance on billing. Staffing stays the chief audit executive's call.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the presumption is real, but it follows the activity Mihi was responsible for. That was patient billing; pharmacy purchasing was never Mihi's.
wrong_explanations.B: Telling the requesting party is the condition for advisory work on a former responsibility. It lifts no presumption, and none applies to an activity Mihi never held.
wrong_explanations.C: Advice with no assurance is what stays open to an auditor on an activity they held within 12 months, after disclosure. Pharmacy purchasing was never Mihi's, so assurance is open.

tips: Eliminate: B, because telling management is the condition for advisory work on a former responsibility, and C, because limiting an auditor to advice matters for an activity they once held.
Final two: D beats A because the presumption follows the activity, not the person's whole past: Mihi held billing, and the engagement is on pharmacy purchasing.
Exam cue: before applying the 12-month presumption, match the activity under review to the activity the auditor was responsible for. No match, no presumption.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. Reviewing one's own workpapers
questions.question: Senior internal auditor Yaw, who has audited a tile maker's inventory for five years, also signed off this year's supervisory review of Yaw's own valuation workpapers. Which risk does that sign-off MOST directly add?

options.A: Assumptions from earlier audits stand in for this year's evidence
options.B: Findings on inventory are filtered before they reach the board
options.C: Errors in Yaw's own valuation work pass the review unnoticed
options.D: Results are shaded to protect Yaw's standing with the tile maker

questions.key_concept: Self-review bias: an auditor reviewing their own work is less critical of it, so errors and gaps are more likely to pass unnoticed.
questions.pre_read: Two biases are in play. Which one comes from the five years, and which from the sign-off?
questions.correct_explanation: The considerations of Standard 2.1 Individual Objectivity name self-review bias and familiarity bias among their examples. Self-review bias: an auditor checking their own work is less critical of it and tends to miss its errors: what Yaw's sign-off adds. Familiarity bias, assumptions carried over from past experience, is the runner-up: five years on one audit make it a real risk here, but it was present before the sign-off and is not caused by it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: five years on the same audit do invite familiarity bias, but that risk was there already. The sign-off adds a different one: Yaw checking Yaw's own work.
wrong_explanations.B: Filtered results point to a weak reporting line, an independence matter for the function. One auditor reviewing their own workpapers is a threat to that person's objectivity.
wrong_explanations.D: Shading results to protect a relationship describes a conflict of interest. Nothing gives Yaw a stake in the tile maker; the weakness is an uncritical second look.

tips: Eliminate: B, because filtered results are a reporting-line problem for the function, and D, because nothing gives Yaw a personal stake in the tile maker's results.
Final two: C beats A because the question asks what the sign-off adds: reviewing one's own work is self-review bias, while familiarity came with the five years.
Exam cue: own work under review points to self-review bias and missed errors; a long, comfortable history with an area points to familiarity bias and weaker skepticism.

questions.subtopic: 1B6 Confidentiality and proper use of information. Confidentiality and reporting to the board
questions.question: A telecom's chief executive asks chief audit executive Ngozi to keep a significant finding on an executive's severance payment out of the board's report, calling personnel terms confidential. What is Ngozi's BEST response?

options.A: Report the finding to the board, payment included, on limited circulation
options.B: Report the finding to the board in outline, leaving the payment out
options.C: Report the finding to the board where a law compels its disclosure
options.D: Report the finding to senior management and let it brief the board

questions.key_concept: Confidentiality bars disclosure to unauthorized parties; the board is authorized to receive results, so a finding is never withheld from it on that ground.
questions.pre_read: Ask who counts as an unauthorized party here, and whether the board is one of them.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.1 Honesty and Professional Courage forbids leaving pertinent facts out, and Standard 8.1 Board Interaction has the chief audit executive give the board what it needs for oversight, also when senior management disputes a finding. Confidentiality does not change that: Standard 5.2 Protection of Information bars disclosure to unauthorized parties, and the board is not one. An outline without the payment is the runner-up, but it drops the fact the board must weigh.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it sounds proportionate, but the payment is the finding. An outline without it withholds a pertinent fact from the body that oversees executives.
wrong_explanations.C: A legal duty is the test for disclosing to an unauthorized party. The board is an authorized recipient of internal audit results, so no legal duty is needed.
wrong_explanations.D: Senior management receives results too, but it does not decide what the board sees. The chief audit executive reports to the board directly, and here an executive wants the omission.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a legal duty is the test for unauthorized parties, not the board, and D, because the chief audit executive reports to the board directly, not through senior management.
Final two: A beats B because an outline without the payment omits the pertinent fact; confidentiality never keeps a finding from the board.
Exam cue: when confidentiality is offered as a reason to keep something from the board, ask who is unauthorized. Limit the other recipients, not the board.

questions.subtopic: 1B6 Confidentiality and proper use of information. A preservation order at close-out
questions.question: Internal audit's close-out routine deletes surplus data extracts, but as a payroll engagement closes a labor regulator lawfully orders payroll data preserved in every form. What is internal auditor Ife's BEST handling of the extract?

options.A: Delete the extract, since payroll's system still holds the source data
options.B: Keep the records that support the findings and delete the rest
options.C: Keep the whole extract under the function's access controls
options.D: Give the regulator the whole extract with the engagement's results

questions.key_concept: Retention and disposal follow law and regulation as well as policy; a lawful preservation order suspends routine deletion, and the kept data stays protected.
questions.pre_read: Find the fact that changes a normal close-out: who has ordered what, and does it reach internal audit's own copy?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.3 Legal and Ethical Behavior has internal auditors abide by the law. Standard 5.2 Protection of Information applies laws and policies to keeping and disposing of information, and Standard 14.6 Engagement Documentation does the same for retention. The order reaches payroll data in every form, so routine deletion gives way and the whole extract stays. Keeping just the findings' support is the runner-up: sound on a normal close-out, but here it destroys covered data.

wrong_explanations.A: On an ordinary close-out a surplus copy is deleted. Here the order reaches payroll data in every form, and the extract is one of them, whatever payroll's own system holds.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: on a normal close-out this is the careful answer. The order reaches payroll data in every form, so deleting the surplus would destroy what must be kept.
wrong_explanations.D: The order asks for preservation, not production. Sending confidential payroll data outside follows the release route the methodology sets, when a demand is made.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the order reaches payroll data in every form, the extract included, and D, because the order asks for the data to be kept, not sent.
Final two: C beats B because the order reaches payroll data in every form, internal audit's extract included; trimming it to the findings' support would destroy protected data.
Exam cue: a sensible default (delete what is no longer needed) gives way when the stem adds a law or a lawful order. Read for that fact before choosing the tidy option.

questions.subtopic: 1B6 Confidentiality and proper use of information. A former employer's information
questions.question: Internal auditor Farid joined a pharmacy chain from a rival, and a supervisor asks Farid to benchmark with the rival's confidential supplier prices, learned on audits there. Which view of those prices is MOST accurate?

options.A: Usable where the benchmark serves the chain's legitimate objectives
options.B: Usable once the chief audit executive approves the benchmark
options.C: Unusable in assurance work, though usable when advising the chain
options.D: Unusable unless the rival authorizes their release to the chain

questions.key_concept: The duty to protect confidential information follows the internal auditor: what was learned in confidence at one organization is not theirs to use at another.
questions.pre_read: Ask who owns the prices and whether anyone with authority over them has agreed to their use.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 5.2 Protection of Information has internal auditors respect the confidentiality and ownership of what they learn in their work, and bars passing it to unauthorized parties unless a legal or professional duty requires it. A benchmark creates no such duty, so by inference only the rival, as owner, could authorize the chain; Standard 1.3's considerations call unauthorized disclosure discreditable. The chain's benefit, the runner-up, does not make the figures Farid's to share.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: serving the organization's legitimate aims is the test for its own information. These figures were learned in confidence at the rival and are still the rival's.
wrong_explanations.B: The chief audit executive's approval governs how this function releases its own records. It cannot authorize the use of information that belongs to another organization.
wrong_explanations.C: The split between assurance and advice matters for objectivity after a former responsibility. Confidentiality does not vary by service: the prices are the rival's in both.

tips: Eliminate: B, because approval inside this function cannot release another organization's information, and C, because the assurance and advice split belongs to objectivity, not to confidentiality.
Final two: D beats A because the duty runs to the owner of the information; a benefit to Farid's new employer does not authorize using the rival's confidential prices.
Exam cue: ask whose information it is. A benefit to the organization, a supervisor's request or a removed name does not transfer ownership.

questions.subtopic: 1B6 Confidentiality and proper use of information. Outside specialists and protection rules
questions.question: A workers' compensation fund's chief audit executive engages an outside actuary, whose firm applies its own data protection policy, for a claims engagement. Which statement about protecting the claims data is MOST accurate?

options.A: The chief audit executive must accept the actuarial firm's policy as written
options.B: The chief audit executive must hold the actuary to the function's rules
options.C: The claims manager must set the actuary's rules as the data's owner
options.D: The chief audit executive must get an attestation to bind the actuary

questions.key_concept: People assisting the internal audit function, such as outside specialists, are held to the function's information protection rules; the chief audit executive sees to it.
questions.pre_read: Ask whom the actuary is working for on this engagement, and whose protection rules that brings.
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 5.2 Protection of Information an outside helper gets no lighter regime: the chief audit executive must see that anyone who assists the function, a specialist included, works under the safeguards the function itself follows. The actuary is such a helper, so the firm's own policy does not replace them here. Accepting the firm's policy is the runner-up: the firm has one, but this data is protected to the function's standard.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the firm has its own policy, but people assisting the function are held to the function's protection requirements, whatever the firm itself allows.
wrong_explanations.C: Management would set the terms for a consultant it engaged itself. This actuary assists internal audit, so the chief audit executive carries the duty.
wrong_explanations.D: A signed attestation is something the chief audit executive may ask for as evidence. The protection requirements apply to the actuary with or without a signature.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the actuary assists internal audit, not the claims unit, and D, because an attestation is optional evidence, not what makes the rules apply.
Final two: B beats A because helpers are held to the function's protection requirements; the firm's own policy does not displace them.
Exam cue: guest auditors, contractors and outside specialists working for internal audit carry the function's confidentiality duties, and the chief audit executive must ensure it.

questions.subtopic: 1B6 Confidentiality and proper use of information. Personal use without disclosure
questions.question: Internal auditor Sina quotes a design firm's senior pay range, seen in payroll workpapers, without names, when asking the human resources head, who sets those ranges, for a raise. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: It is misuse, since engagement information served a personal gain
options.B: It is proper, since nothing reached an unauthorized party
options.C: It is proper, since nobody was identified or put at a loss
options.D: It is misuse, since pay data was disclosed without authorization

questions.key_concept: Using engagement information for personal gain is misuse in itself, even when nothing is disclosed to an unauthorized party and nobody is harmed.
questions.pre_read: Separate two questions: who learned the information, and what was it used for?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 5.1 Use of Information bars internal auditors from using information for personal gain, and that test is about use, not about who else learns it or who loses. Sina took the pay range from engagement workpapers to strengthen a personal pay claim, so it is misuse although human resources already knew the figures. That nothing was disclosed is the runner-up: correct under Standard 5.2 Protection of Information, but disclosure is a separate rule.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: no unauthorized party learned anything, so the disclosure rule is not broken. The separate rule against using information for personal gain is.
wrong_explanations.C: Harm and naming matter when judging a privacy exposure. The bar on personal gain does not depend on anyone losing or being identified.
wrong_explanations.D: The human resources head sets the ranges and is entitled to the figures, so nothing was disclosed without authorization. The fault lies in what Sina used them for.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the bar on personal gain needs no victim, and D, because the human resources head is entitled to pay data, so nothing was disclosed without authorization.
Final two: A beats B because use and disclosure are separate rules: nothing was disclosed, yet engagement information still served Sina's own benefit.
Exam cue: test information questions twice. Was it disclosed to someone unauthorized? Was it used for anything but the work? Either one is enough.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Acting with integrity. A material fact outside the engagement's scope
questions.question: A Thai manufacturer's senior management renews a supplier's contract next week; in a travel-claims audit reporting next month, internal auditor Somchai finds a certifier's notice withdrawing that supplier's safety approval. What is Somchai's BEST course?

options.A: Have it reported in the final communication, marked as outside the scope
options.B: Have the chief audit executive widen the scope, and test it first
options.C: Raise it at once with the chief audit executive, to pass upward
options.D: Raise it at once with the travel-claims managers, to pass upward

questions.key_concept: A material fact must be disclosed even when it lies outside the engagement's scope; the decision it could change sets how soon and to whom.
questions.pre_read: Ask who needs this fact, and by when, before asking where it fits in the engagement.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.1 Honesty and Professional Courage requires disclosing material facts whose absence could weaken the organization's decisions, with no scope limit. It names no recipient or deadline; the pending decision sets both. Senior management decides next week, and Standard 7.1's essential conditions place the chief audit executive to take matters straight to senior management. The travel-claims managers, the runner-up, act in time but neither own nor make this decision.

wrong_explanations.A: It does disclose the fact, but in a communication due weeks after senior management renews. The duty exists so that decisions are made knowing the facts.
wrong_explanations.B: A scope change, which Standard 13.3 has the chief audit executive approve, suits matters needing tests. A certifier's notice is independent evidence already, and testing first risks missing the renewal.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it acts in time, as Standard 13.1's considerations do for urgent issues in the activity audited. The contract is not that activity, and not those managers' decision.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the final communication arrives after the renewal, and B, because the certifier's notice already establishes the fact and disclosure does not wait on testing.
Final two: C beats D because both act at once, but the contract is senior management's decision, and the chief audit executive is positioned to take matters straight to senior management.
Exam cue: scope limits what an engagement tests, not what an internal auditor must speak up about. Look for who is about to decide, and who can reach them in time.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Acting with integrity. A designation shown while inactive
questions.question: Internal auditor Obinna's certification became inactive in March because education hours went unreported, yet the designation still follows Obinna's name on engagement communications at a Nigerian broadcaster. What is Obinna's BEST course with the designation?

options.A: Remove it until the certifying body restores the active status
options.B: Remove it, and step off engagements until the status is restored
options.C: Keep it, and report the overdue hours within the quarter
options.D: Keep it, and tell the chief audit executive about the lapse

questions.key_concept: Showing a certification that is lapsed or inactive misstates a qualification, discreditable under the Standards; the letters stay off until it is active again.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a reader of the signature is led to believe, and whether that is true today.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.3 Legal and Ethical Behavior bars discreditable conduct, and its considerations give showing a lapsed or inactive designation as an example of misstating a qualification. Standard 1.1 Honesty and Professional Courage bars misleading statements in any case. So the letters come off until the status is active again. Catching up while keeping them is the runner-up: Standard 3.2 Continuing Professional Development requires it, but meanwhile the signature claims a status Obinna lacks.

wrong_explanations.B: Certification is not what admits an internal auditor to engagements; competency is. Stepping off suits a role that requires an active designation, which ordinary engagement work does not.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the hours must be reported, but until the certifying body restores the status it is inactive, and the signature claims otherwise.
wrong_explanations.D: Telling the chief audit executive is candid, but readers of the communications still see a designation that is not currently valid.

tips: Eliminate: B, because competency, not certification, is what engagement work requires, and D, because telling the chief audit executive leaves the misleading designation in front of readers.
Final two: A beats C because reporting the hours fixes the cause later; meanwhile the signature would still claim a status that is not active.
Exam cue: a credential is a statement of fact about today. Expired, inactive, revoked or never earned all lead to the same answer: do not display it.
