questions.subtopic: 1B3 Policies and safeguards for objectivity. The only specialist is impaired
questions.question: A Chilean fund's board wants derivatives valuations assured within seven months; Rodrigo, internal audit's only specialist, headed valuations until five months ago; another specialist joins next month. What is the chief audit executive's BEST response?

options.A: Take Rodrigo off, and reschedule the work for the incoming expert
options.B: Take Rodrigo off, and limit the scope to what others can test
options.C: Keep Rodrigo testing, under the chief audit executive's close review
options.D: Keep Rodrigo testing, after disclosing the former role to the board

questions.key_concept: An impaired expert comes off assurance on a recent former responsibility; the time and staffing facts then pick among the unranked remedies.
questions.pre_read: Two needs pull apart here: objectivity and expertise. Check which options meet both, and by when.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity bars internal auditors from assessing an activity they used to run, and presumes impairment for assurance within 12 months; five months is inside that, and expertise does not cancel it. Standard 2.3's considerations offer reassigning, rescheduling, rescoping or outsourcing, unranked. Here a specialist arrives next month with six months left, so rescheduling delivers the full scope the board asked for; narrowing, the runner-up, would drop it.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: rescoping is a listed option, and Standard 13.5's considerations allow it when resources cannot be had. A specialist arrives next month; narrowing drops the board's request.
wrong_explanations.C: Review can mitigate some threats, but Standard 2.2 requires refraining from assessing one's former responsibility. A reviewed assessment of one's own former desk is still self-review.
wrong_explanations.D: Disclosing to the requesting party is the condition for advisory work on a former responsibility. Assurance is different: Rodrigo must refrain, whoever has been told.

tips: Eliminate: C, because review does not lift the duty to refrain from assessing a former responsibility, and D, because disclosure is the condition for advisory work, not assurance.
Final two: A beats B because both remove Rodrigo, but a specialist arrives next month with six months left, so rescheduling keeps the full scope the board asked for.
Exam cue: when the only expert is impaired, remove the person first, then choose among reassign, reschedule, rescope or outsource by the stem's facts: who is free, by when, and what was asked.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Policies and safeguards for objectivity. The chief audit executive's own impairment
questions.question: Chief audit executive Wambui's sibling becomes procurement head at a Kenyan coffee cooperative; no procurement audit is planned, and any impairment is in appearance only. Which disclosure do the Standards MOST clearly require of Wambui?

options.A: To procurement's management, when an audit there is next planned
options.B: To the board, if senior management cannot settle the concern
options.C: To senior management, with the reasons the exposure is minimal
options.D: To the board, whatever senior management makes of the concern

questions.key_concept: The chief audit executive's own impairment, in fact or in appearance alone, must be disclosed to the board; other recipients belong to other cases.
questions.pre_read: Whose objectivity is in question? The answer to that decides who has to be told.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.3 Disclosing Impairments to Objectivity gives each case its recipient. An internal auditor tells the chief audit executive or a designated supervisor; a chief audit executive whose own objectivity is affected tells the board, whether in fact or in appearance. Senior management is the runner-up: the considerations let a perception-only concern raised in engagement planning be explained to management and documented, but that option does not replace the board for Wambui's own impairment.

wrong_explanations.A: Talking to the activity's management is an option for a perception-only concern met in engagement planning. It is not the disclosure Standard 2.3 requires for Wambui's own impairment.
wrong_explanations.B: Senior management first, then the board if unresolved, is Standard 11.5's order for risk that management has accepted. Wambui's own impairment goes to the board without that filter.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: at engagement planning, a perception-only concern may be explained to management and documented. That option cannot replace the required disclosure of Wambui's own impairment to the board.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the activity's management is an option for planning-stage concerns about perception, and B, because senior management first is the order for accepted risk, not for this disclosure.
Final two: D beats C because appearance alone still triggers the rule for the chief audit executive's own impairment, and that rule names the board.
Exam cue: match the impaired person to the recipient. An auditor tells the chief audit executive or a designated supervisor; the chief audit executive tells the board.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Policies and safeguards for objectivity. Two gift policies that differ
questions.question: A Polish bookseller's staff conduct code bans all supplier gifts; its audit manual allows small ones from parties not under review. Which rule BEST settles whether internal auditor Kasia may keep an unaudited supplier's calendar?

options.A: The audit manual, which the function wrote for its own auditors
options.B: The bookseller's conduct code, which binds each of its employees
options.C: The Standards' objectivity test, which every gift has to pass
options.D: The chief audit executive's ruling on which document applies

questions.key_concept: Internal auditors must meet the organization's ethical expectations; a permission in the audit manual does not lift a ban in the organization's code.
questions.pre_read: Two rulebooks cover this calendar. Ask whether passing one of them is enough.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.2 Organization's Ethical Expectations requires internal auditors to meet the organization's legitimate conduct rules, so the code's ban reaches Kasia like any employee. Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity's considerations apply the same logic where the audit policy is the stricter one: auditors should then keep to the stricter. Relying on the manual is the runner-up: a function may set tighter rules for its auditors, but its manual cannot release them from the code.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: auditors must follow the function's manual, but it only permits small gifts; declining breaks neither rulebook, while keeping one breaks a ban that covers every employee.
wrong_explanations.C: Every gift has to pass the objectivity test in Standard 2.2, but passing it is not permission. What the organization's code bans stays banned.
wrong_explanations.D: A ruling cannot lift the ban: Standard 1.2 has every internal auditor, the chief audit executive included, meet the organization's conduct rules.

tips: Eliminate: C, because passing the objectivity test does not override the organization's code, and D, because no ruling by the chief audit executive can permit what that code bans.
Final two: B beats A because Standard 4.1 has auditors follow the manual, but the manual only permits; declining the calendar keeps both rulebooks.
Exam cue: when two conduct rules apply to an internal auditor, a permission in one never cancels a ban in the other. Keep to the ban.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. A shorter version for the board
questions.question: Keeping every finding, rating, conclusion and action plan, internal auditor Losana condenses the detailed fuel-card communication written for a Fijian cannery's transport manager into one page for the board. Which view is MOST accurate?

options.A: Improper: the board is owed the same communication the manager received
options.B: Improper: dropping detail the manager received omits pertinent information
options.C: Proper: each reader gets what that reader needs in order to act
options.D: Proper: findings rated below high need not go to the board

questions.key_concept: Fitting the detail to each reader is expected; honesty is broken when a finding or other pertinent information is left out.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the board's page drops with what the board needs for its own decisions.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 11.2 Effective Communication's considerations say internal auditors should adapt a communication to its recipient and to the actions that recipient is responsible for, and Standard 15.1 Final Engagement Communication's allow versions with different detail. Standard 1.1 Honesty and Professional Courage bars leaving out findings or pertinent information, and the page keeps every finding, rating, conclusion and action plan. So the omission view, the runner-up, fails: supporting detail is not what the board acts on.

wrong_explanations.A: Standard 11.4 sends one correction to everyone who received the original when a significant error is found. First communications may differ by reader.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: leaving out a finding or a pertinent fact would breach Standard 1.1. Here every finding, rating, conclusion and action plan stays; only supporting detail is shorter.
wrong_explanations.D: What reaches the board follows the board's expectations, which Standard 11.3 has the chief audit executive understand. Here no finding was dropped, so a rating cut-off is not the reason.

tips: Eliminate: A, because one text for all applies to corrections of significant errors, and D, because no finding was dropped, so a rating cut-off explains nothing here.
Final two: C beats B because omission means losing a finding or a pertinent fact; shortening supporting detail for a reader who does not need it is fitting the message.
Exam cue: ask what was removed. A finding, rating or conclusion dropped to soften the message is omission; detail trimmed to suit the reader is good communication.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. Informal contact and objectivity
questions.question: Fearing bias, internal auditor Jamal wants to stop the monthly informal catch-ups with a Jordanian bottling plant's shift supervisors that the function's stakeholder approach calls for. Which reply from the chief audit executive is BEST?

options.A: Stop them: distance from audited staff keeps objectivity intact
options.B: Replace them with minuted formal meetings: a record can keep contact proper
options.C: Keep them: rotating auditors among divisions can guard objectivity
options.D: Keep them: disclosing each as a possible impairment can cover the risk

questions.key_concept: The Standards expect regular informal contact with stakeholders; objectivity is protected by means such as rotation, not by keeping a distance.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the informal contact is for, and whether objectivity has other protections.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 11.1 Building Relationships and Communicating with Stakeholders requires the chief audit executive to promote informal as well as formal communication. Its considerations explain why: steady informal contact builds the trust that brings candid talk formal meetings may not, and rotating auditors among units may balance that benefit against objectivity. Minuted formal meetings are the runner-up: they keep contact, but lose the candor the informal kind exists to earn.

wrong_explanations.A: Distance is not the Standards' safeguard. Standard 2.1 asks for an unbiased mindset and managed biases, while Standard 11.1 expects relationships with stakeholders.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: formal meetings have their place, but the Standards call for informal contact too, because it earns the trust and candor a minuted meeting rarely does.
wrong_explanations.D: Standard 2.3 requires disclosing an impairment, such as a close personal tie (an example in Standard 2.2's considerations). Routine contact set by the function's own approach is not one.

tips: Eliminate: A, because relationships with stakeholders are expected and distance is not the safeguard, and D, because routine working contact is not an impairment to disclose.
Final two: C beats B because the Standards want informal contact as well as formal; rotation, not formality, is a way they name to balance it with objectivity.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, objectivity is rarely protected by avoiding people. Look for rotation, disclosure or reassignment, with the working relationship kept.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. A new subject under an expert supervisor
questions.question: To broaden experience, a New Zealand orchard's chief audit executive assigns internal auditor Kiri, who has never audited customs duties, to a customs engagement supervised by an experienced customs auditor. What is Kiri's BEST response?

options.A: Accept, and build the knowledge while the engagement proceeds
options.B: Accept, but leave the steps that need customs knowledge to others
options.C: Hold off until a course on customs duties has been completed
options.D: Raise it with the chief audit executive as a resource shortfall

questions.key_concept: Internal auditors may take on work they can become competent for; new knowledge may be built on an engagement under proper supervision.
questions.pre_read: Check who on this engagement already has the knowledge, and what that person's role is.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 3.1 Competency lets internal auditors take on services they can attain the competencies for, and its considerations count new tasks done under supervision among the ways to develop them. The supervisor has the knowledge, so nothing is missing from the team. Raising a resource shortfall is the runner-up, but Standard 13.5 Engagement Resources requires that step when resources are inappropriate or insufficient, and these are neither.

wrong_explanations.B: Avoiding the customs steps would defeat the assignment. With a supervisor who has the knowledge, Kiri can perform them and learn while the supervisor guides and reviews the work.
wrong_explanations.C: A course is one way to build competency, not a condition. Standard 3.2's considerations count properly supervised engagement work as another, and it is available here.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a gap nobody on the engagement can cover goes to the chief audit executive. Here the supervisor covers it, and the chief audit executive made the assignment.

tips: Eliminate: B, because supervised work on the customs steps is how the knowledge is built, and C, because a course is one route to competency, not a condition.
Final two: A beats D because the engagement's resources are sufficient: the supervisor holds the knowledge, so there is no shortfall to raise.
Exam cue: check whether the missing skill is missing from one auditor or from the whole team. The second is a resource gap; the first is a chance to learn.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Due professional care and skepticism. Significance relative to the activity
questions.question: Planning an Indian hospital group's laundry audit, internal auditor Kavita finds linen losses worth a fifth of the laundry unit's budget but trivial to the group. Which view of that risk is MOST accurate?

options.A: Minor: materiality is measured against the organization as a whole
options.B: Minor: care weighs the cost of testing against the possible loss
options.C: Significant: losses of assets are fraud risks, which take priority
options.D: Significant: it is weighed against the unit under review's objectives

questions.key_concept: Significance is relative: a risk small for the organization can be significant to the activity under review, and the engagement risk assessment judges it there.
questions.pre_read: Whose objectives does an engagement risk assessment look at? Size the loss against those.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 4.2 Due Professional Care has internal auditors assess how material or significant risks are to the activity under review, and its considerations add that a risk can be minor for the organization yet significant in an engagement. Standard 13.2 Engagement Risk Assessment ranks risks to that activity's objectives. A fifth of the unit's budget is significant there. Group-level materiality is the runner-up: it suits the organization-wide assessment behind the plan, not this one.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: size against the whole organization matters when the internal audit plan is built under Standard 9.4. An engagement risk assessment weighs risks against the activity under review.
wrong_explanations.B: Cost against benefit helps decide how much work a risk deserves. It does not make a loss of a fifth of the unit's budget minor.
wrong_explanations.C: Fraud risk has to be considered in every engagement risk assessment, then ranked by significance like any other risk. No rule puts every loss of assets first.

tips: Eliminate: B, because cost against benefit sets how much work a risk gets, not its significance, and C, because fraud risk must be considered, not automatically ranked first.
Final two: D beats A because an engagement risk assessment weighs risks against the activity under review; group-level size belongs to the plan's risk assessment.
Exam cue: before rating a risk, ask 'significant to what?' When planning an engagement the answer is the activity under review and its objectives.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Due professional care and skepticism. Two figures that disagree
questions.question: Internal auditor Soo-min's own extract from a Korean steel mill's learning system shows 81% of staff completed safety training, but the safety manager's dashboard shows 98%. What should Soo-min do FIRST?

options.A: Rerun the extract, and use its figure if the result repeats
options.B: Ask the manager about the gap, and trace both figures to source
options.C: Ask the manager which figure is right, and use that one
options.D: Report the dashboard as misleading, since the extract contradicts it

questions.key_concept: Skepticism covers the auditor's own data too: an inconsistency is raised openly and resolved with further evidence before either figure is relied on.
questions.pre_read: Two sources disagree. Before choosing one, ask what could make each of them wrong.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 4.3 Professional Skepticism has internal auditors ask about inconsistent information in a straightforward way and seek more evidence before judging it. Either figure could be wrong: the extract may use the wrong dates or staff list, or the dashboard may be overstated. Rerunning the extract is the runner-up: Standard 14.1 Gathering Information for Analyses and Evaluation rates directly obtained information as more reliable, but the same query repeats the same answer.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: checking one's own work is sound, and directly obtained information is more reliable in general. But the same query repeats the same answer; the gap stays unexplained.
wrong_explanations.C: Asking is right; settling the matter on the manager's word is not. A statement about which figure is correct still needs evidence behind it.
wrong_explanations.D: Calling information misleading is a conclusion, and it needs evidence. Until the gap is explained, nothing shows which figure is wrong, or why.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the manager's word on which figure is right is not evidence, and D, because calling the dashboard misleading is a conclusion reached before the evidence.
Final two: B beats A because a rerun repeats the extract's own assumptions; an unexplained gap is resolved by asking openly and tracing both figures.
Exam cue: when two sources disagree, CIA answers neither pick a side on trust nor accuse. They ask openly and reconcile both to source records.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Acting with integrity. An ethics concern about the board chair
questions.question: A Botswana bank's board chair took a borrower-paid holiday, breaching the code of conduct but no law; no policy says who hears concerns about directors. To whom should the chief audit executive BEST report it?

options.A: The audit committee, which oversees the internal audit function
options.B: The chief executive officer, who administers the bank's code of conduct
options.C: The banking regulator, which approves the bank's directors
options.D: The whole board, which the chair also sits on

questions.key_concept: When an ethics concern involves the board chair and no policy covers it, the chief audit executive should report it to the entire board.
questions.pre_read: Who is involved decides who hears an ethics concern. Check first what the organization's policy covers.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.2 Organization's Ethical Expectations requires reporting conduct that breaks the organization's ethical expectations as its policies direct, and no policy here covers directors. The considerations then guide the chief audit executive by seniority: misconduct by senior management goes to the board, and anything touching the chair goes to every director. The audit committee, the runner-up, is internal audit's usual line to the board, but this concern is for all directors.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the audit committee is internal audit's usual route to the board. For a concern involving the board chair, the considerations to Standard 1.2 name the entire board.
wrong_explanations.B: The chief executive officer answers to the board its chair leads. Sending a concern about the chair there puts it below the person it concerns.
wrong_explanations.C: Standard 1.3 sends legal or regulatory violations to whoever has authority to act. The stem rules out any law being broken, so this concern is not the regulator's to hear.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a concern about the board chair cannot go to someone who answers to the board, and C, because the stem says no law was broken, so no legal duty sends it outside.
Final two: D beats A because, with no policy covering directors, the considerations to Standard 1.2 send a concern about the chair to the entire board, not to one committee.
Exam cue: match the recipient to who is involved: staff as policy directs, a senior manager to the board, the board chair to the whole board.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Acting with integrity. An auditor's own error shown at the closing meeting
questions.question: A Jordanian hotel's finance manager shows internal auditor Rania, at the closing meeting, approvals in another system for 9 of the 12 refunds Rania's draft calls unapproved; Rania verifies them. What is Rania's BEST course?

options.A: Keep the finding, and record both positions under the methodology
options.B: Revise the finding to the three refunds, and own the miss
options.C: Keep the finding, as results need not change after a disagreement
options.D: Withdraw the finding on the refunds, and own the miss

questions.key_concept: Verified evidence of an error is a valid reason to change a result: correct the finding to what the evidence shows, and own the error.
questions.pre_read: Is there a valid reason to change the result here? If so, how far should the change go?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.1 Honesty and Professional Courage requires accurate communications, and Standard 13.1 lets internal auditors keep results unchanged only when there is no valid reason to change them. Verified approvals are such a reason, so the finding shrinks to the three refunds still unapproved, and Rania names the miss as Rania's own: Standard 1.3 counts failing to accept responsibility for mistakes as discreditable. Withdrawing the finding, the runner-up, would drop three real exceptions.

wrong_explanations.A: Recording both positions fits a disagreement with no new evidence. Here the evidence is verified and shows the draft was wrong, which is a valid reason to change it.
wrong_explanations.C: Standard 13.1 protects results from change without a valid reason. Verified approvals for nine refunds are such a reason, so keeping the draft would state something inaccurate.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: owning the error is right, but three refunds still lack approval. Withdrawing the whole finding would leave out exceptions the evidence supports.

tips: Eliminate: A and C, because both keep a draft that verified approvals have shown to be wrong, and evidence of an error is a valid reason to change results.
Final two: B beats D because correcting an error means stating the condition accurately: three refunds still lack approval, so the finding shrinks rather than disappears.
Exam cue: when new evidence is verified, change the result to match it, no more and no less; when only opinion is offered, the result stands.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Acting with integrity. A host country's law the home country does not share
questions.question: Internal auditor Arif finds a Singapore shipper's Jakarta subsidiary sending data abroad as Singapore law allows but Indonesian law forbids; neither law obliges staff to report it. Which view is MOST accurate?

options.A: A violation, to report straight to Indonesia's data regulator
options.B: Not a violation, as the group follows Singapore's law
options.C: A violation, to report as the group's own policies direct
options.D: Not a violation, as the engagement's criteria are group policies

questions.key_concept: Internal auditors heed the laws of every jurisdiction the organization operates in, and report a violation by the route laws and policies set.
questions.pre_read: Whose law governs work done in another country? Then ask whether any law says who must be told.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.3 Legal and Ethical Behavior requires internal auditors to know and follow the laws of the organization's industry and of each place it operates, so Indonesian law governs the Jakarta subsidiary whatever Singapore allows. A violation then goes to people with authority to act, by the route laws, regulations and policies set. No law obliges staff to tell the regulator, so the group's policies decide; going straight to the regulator, the runner-up, skips them.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: an outside authority is told when a law or regulation requires it. Neither law obliges staff to report here, so the group's policies set the route.
wrong_explanations.B: Standard 1.3 covers the laws of every place the organization operates. The subsidiary works in Indonesia, so Singapore's permission does not make the transfer lawful there.
wrong_explanations.D: Group policies are common engagement criteria, but the law binds the organization whatever the criteria say. Breaking Indonesian law is a violation even outside them.

tips: Eliminate: B and D, because Standard 1.3 reaches the laws of every country the organization operates in, whatever the home country allows or the engagement's criteria say.
Final two: C beats A because a violation goes where laws and policies direct; with no law requiring staff to tell the regulator, the group's policies set the route.
Exam cue: first ask whose law applies where the activity happens; then ask whether any law names who must be told. If none does, follow policy.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Policies and safeguards for objectivity. An impairment in appearance only, raised at planning
questions.question: Planning a Croatian ferry line's fuel audit, the chief audit executive judges internal auditor Luka's apartment-sharing with the fuel manager, a decade ago, raises an appearance concern only. Which step BEST supports keeping Luka on?

options.A: Disclose the tie to the board, and minute its approval to proceed
options.B: Tell fuel's managers why the risk is small, and record the decision
options.C: Have Luka sign a no-conflict declaration, and file it with the workpapers
options.D: Have an outside provider supervise Luka's work, and record the decision

questions.key_concept: For a planning-stage concern about appearance alone, the chief audit executive may explain to the activity's management why exposure is minimal and document the decision.
questions.pre_read: An appearance concern is about how others see the work. Who needs to be told, and what record is kept?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.3 Disclosing Impairments to Objectivity has the internal auditor disclose an impairment to the chief audit executive, who determines the action. When a concern raised at planning rests on perception alone, the considerations offer a lighter route: talk it through with the activity's managers, say why exposure is low, and record the outcome. Board approval, the runner-up, hands the board a staffing decision the chief audit executive owns.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the chief audit executive may consult the board on a staff auditor's impairment, but determines the action; the Standards ask for no board approval here.
wrong_explanations.C: A signed declaration records Luka's own view in the file. An appearance concern turns on how others see the tie, so it is explained to them and recorded.
wrong_explanations.D: Outside supervision is an option for an impairment that cannot be avoided. For a concern of appearance alone, it adds cost without addressing how others see Luka's role.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a declaration by Luka does not address how others see the tie, and D, because outside supervision answers impairments that cannot otherwise be managed.

Final two: B beats A because the chief audit executive, not the board, decides how a staff auditor's impairment is handled; for a planning-stage perception concern, explaining and recording it is enough.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Policies and safeguards for objectivity. A supervisor with a recent former responsibility
questions.question: Audit manager Priya ran a Malaysian airline's catering purchasing until eight months ago and will supervise this quarter's assurance engagement on it, performed by two unconnected auditors. What is the chief audit executive's BEST course?

options.A: Keep Priya supervising, as the testers are unimpaired
options.B: Keep Priya supervising, once catering's managers are told
options.C: Remove Priya, and let the senior tester supervise the engagement
options.D: Remove Priya, and give the supervision to an untied audit manager

questions.key_concept: Supervising is assessing: whoever approves the work and its conclusions must also be free of a recent responsibility for the activity.
questions.pre_read: Who shapes this engagement's conclusions besides the auditors who test? Check each person against the former-responsibility rule.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity bars internal auditors from assessing activities they were responsible for and presumes impairment in assurance work within 12 months. A supervisor who approves the work and its conclusions is assessing it, and the considerations ask that those who perform and those who supervise both be independent of the activity. Reassignment, listed in Standard 2.3, fixes it. Unimpaired testers, the runner-up, still leave Priya's review in charge.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Priya would approve the testers' work and conclusions. The considerations to Standard 2.2 ask that supervisors, too, be free of the activity; eight months is inside the presumption.
wrong_explanations.B: Telling the requester fits advisory work on a former responsibility; explaining to management fits appearance-only concerns. Assurance on a role Priya left eight months ago fits neither.
wrong_explanations.C: Removing Priya is right, but the senior tester would then approve their own tests, which is self-review bias. Supervision should come from someone outside the testing.

tips: Eliminate: B, because telling management does not lift a presumed impairment in assurance work, and C, because a tester supervising their own tests reviews their own work.
Final two: D beats A because supervising is assessing: whoever approves the work and conclusions should also be free of the activity, not only those who test.
Exam cue: check every person who shapes the conclusion, supervisor included, against the former-responsibility rule, not only the staff doing the testing.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Policies and safeguards for objectivity. Nobody inside is free, and the deadline is near
questions.question: A Uruguayan port's board needs assurance on billing for a regulator this quarter; chief audit executive Inés's spouse heads billing, and Inés's one auditor ran billing until five months ago. What is Inés's BEST course?

options.A: Disclose to the board, and outsource performing and supervising it
options.B: Disclose to the board, and reschedule until a new auditor joins
options.C: Disclose to the board, and perform the engagement personally
options.D: Disclose to the board, and outsource the supervision

questions.key_concept: When everyone inside is impaired and the work cannot wait, outsiders perform and supervise it; the chief audit executive's own impairment goes to the board.
questions.pre_read: List who is impaired, who is free, and the deadline. Then see which option is left.
questions.correct_explanation: Both people are impaired. The auditor ran billing five months ago, so Standard 2.2 presumes impairment for assurance, and the chief audit executive's spouse heads billing, a conflict Standard 2.3 requires disclosing to the board. Its considerations list outsourcing performance or supervision; with the deadline this quarter and nobody unimpaired inside, an outside provider doing both fits. Disclosing and then performing it personally, the runner-up, leaves the conflict in the work.

wrong_explanations.B: Rescheduling fits when the deadline allows waiting for unimpaired staff. The regulator needs assurance this quarter, so waiting for a hire misses it.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: disclosing to the board is required, but disclosure does not remove a conflict. Assessing a unit the spouse heads would leave the results open to doubt.
wrong_explanations.D: Outsourcing supervision alone fits when only the supervisor is impaired. The auditor ran billing five months ago, so the person testing must also be free of it.

tips: Eliminate: B, because waiting for a hire misses the regulator's deadline this quarter, and D, because outside supervision alone leaves the tester's recent responsibility in place.
Final two: A beats C because disclosure is required of the chief audit executive but does not remove the spouse's conflict; with nobody free inside, outsiders do the work.
Exam cue: when nobody inside is free and time is short, outsourcing is the option the facts leave; disclosure is still owed, but it is not the safeguard.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. Borrowed expertise with a tie to the subject
questions.question: Chief audit executive Ama is staffing a Kenyan insurer's claims-reserve assurance engagement, starting in six weeks; no internal auditor knows reserving, and the risk function's actuary signs off the reserves. Which expertise source is BEST?

options.A: The risk function's actuary, seconded as a guest auditor
options.B: An internal auditor learning reserving as fieldwork proceeds
options.C: An outside actuarial firm, hired under contract for this work
options.D: The firm that built the reserving model, hired under a contract

questions.key_concept: Obtain missing competencies from an expert free of the subject: someone who signs off an activity cannot help assure it.
questions.pre_read: Two things matter in borrowed expertise: can the person do the work, and are they free of it?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 3.1 Competency requires the chief audit executive to obtain competencies the function lacks, and the considerations to Standards 3.1 and 10.2 list sources from guest auditors to outside providers. The risk function's actuary, the runner-up, signs off the reserves under review, so seconding them would mean assessing their own work, which Standard 2.2 rules out for anyone providing internal audit services. An outside firm with no part in the model avoids that tie.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the considerations to Standard 10.2 let an in-house expert serve as a guest auditor, but this actuary signs off the reserves, so they would assess their own work.
wrong_explanations.B: Learning on an engagement suits an auditor supervised by someone who knows the area. Nobody in the function knows reserving, so no one could guide or check the work.
wrong_explanations.D: An outside firm is a source the considerations to Standard 3.1 name, but this one built the model under review, so it would be assessing its own work.

tips: Eliminate: B, because learning on the job needs a supervisor who knows the area, and nobody here does, and D, because the model's builder would be reviewing its own work.
Final two: C beats A because a guest auditor must be free of the subject too; the actuary signs off the reserves being assured, while this outside firm has no such tie.
Exam cue: when borrowing expertise, test the expert's tie to the subject as you would an auditor's: competent and objective, not competent alone.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. Management's cheaper fix that does the same job
questions.question: Internal auditor Bongani recommended a module blocking a Zambian mine's unapproved overtime; payroll's manager offers a current-system setting that Bongani confirms does the same for a tenth of the cost. What is Bongani's BEST course?

options.A: Keep the module, and ask senior management to choose
options.B: Agree the setting as management's action plan for the finding
options.C: Report the module's rejection to senior management as accepted risk
options.D: Agree the setting for now, if the module is bought next year

questions.key_concept: Negotiation aims at an action that fixes the finding at sensible cost; when management's alternative does the same job more cheaply, the auditor agrees it.
questions.pre_read: What was the recommendation for? Check whether management's plan achieves that, and at what cost.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.4 Recommendations and Action Plans lets internal auditors develop recommendations, request action plans or agree actions with management, and its considerations weigh feasibility, cost against benefit and whether the risk is brought within tolerance. The setting blocks unapproved overtime as the module would, at a tenth of the cost, so agreeing it is the sound outcome. Asking senior management to choose, the runner-up, fits only where the parties still differ on substance.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: in a real disagreement, the chief audit executive involves senior management under Standard 14.4's considerations. Bongani confirmed the setting does the same job, so nothing needs resolving.
wrong_explanations.C: Risk acceptance arises when management leaves a risk above appetite or tolerance. The setting blocks unapproved overtime, so no risk is being accepted.
wrong_explanations.D: A condition fits when a quick fix is only temporary. The setting does the full job, so tying it to next year's purchase adds cost without benefit.

tips: Eliminate: C, because no risk is left above tolerance when the setting blocks the overtime, and D, because a complete fix needs no purchase attached to it.
Final two: B beats A because no disagreement is left to escalate; negotiation aims at an action that fixes the finding at sensible cost, not a win for the first recommendation.
Exam cue: when management's alternative meets the same objective more cheaply, agree it; keep pressing only when the alternative leaves the risk unaddressed.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. Ethics training for an auditor without IIA certification
questions.question: Internal auditor Mateo holds an accounting designation but no IIA certification and says ethics training is only for IIA certificate holders. Which reply from Mateo's chief audit executive at a Colombian bank is MOST accurate?

options.A: The Standards require it yearly of every internal auditor, Mateo included
options.B: The Standards recommend it for every internal auditor, Mateo included
options.C: The Standards leave it to IIA certificate holders, as Mateo says
options.D: The Standards defer to the accounting body's ethics rules for Mateo

questions.key_concept: Development is required of every internal auditor; ethics-focused training is required through IIA certification and recommended for every other internal auditor.
questions.pre_read: Separate what is required of everyone, what a certification requires, and what is only recommended.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 3.2 Continuing Professional Development requires every internal auditor to keep developing through education and training, and requires certified auditors to meet their certification's rules, which for The IIA's certifications include ethics training. Its considerations then extend the expectation, as a recommendation, to everyone else in the profession. So for Mateo it is recommended, not required by the Standards; a yearly requirement, the runner-up, overstates a 'should'.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: development itself is required of everyone under Standard 3.2, but ethics-focused training for auditors without IIA certification is a 'should', with no yearly amount set.
wrong_explanations.C: The requirement does come from IIA certification policies, but the considerations to Standard 3.2 extend the expectation to all internal auditors, so Mateo is not outside it.
wrong_explanations.D: Domain II still applies to internal auditors who follow another code. Another body's rules add to the Standards' expectations; they do not replace them.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the expectation of ethics training reaches all internal auditors, and D, because another body's code never displaces Domain II for an internal auditor.
Final two: B beats A because ethics-focused training is a 'should' for auditors without IIA certification; development in general and a certification's own rules are the 'musts'.
Exam cue: when an option says 'required', check whether the Standards say must or should for that exact person; a recommendation stated as a rule is a trap.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Due professional care and skepticism. A tool that can test the whole population
questions.question: The function's analytics tool can query all 1.8 million meal-allowance claims at a Kazakh haulier, where internal auditor Dmitri is planning a test for duplicate claims. Which approach BEST fits due professional care?

options.A: A tool-drawn statistical sample, with the error rate projected
options.B: Management's monthly duplicate-claims exception report, reviewed for gaps
options.C: Software matching across every claim, with each match followed up
options.D: A walkthrough of how the system blocks duplicate claims

questions.key_concept: Due care weighs which techniques and tools fit; when software can test a whole population cheaply, and errors hide between items, full-population analysis beats sampling.
questions.pre_read: What does a duplicate look like in the data? Ask which approach could actually find one.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 4.2 Due Professional Care has internal auditors weigh which techniques and tools suit the work, and its cost against its benefit, and the considerations to Standard 14.1 note that analysis software makes testing a whole population practical. The test's aim is to find duplicates paid; a sample, the runner-up, would only estimate how many, while matching every claim finds each one at little extra cost.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the tool can draw samples, and sampling suits many tests. But a projected rate only estimates duplicates; matching every claim finds each one paid, at little extra cost.
wrong_explanations.B: A management report could support reliance where its controls are known to work. Duplicates are the very risk under test, so the report is not independent evidence of it.
wrong_explanations.D: A walkthrough shows how the control is meant to work, which suits planning. It cannot show whether duplicate claims were paid, which is what this test seeks.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a report from the activity under review is not independent evidence of its own risk, and D, because a walkthrough shows design, not whether duplicates were paid.
Final two: C beats A because the aim is to find each duplicate paid; a sample only estimates the rate, while the tool can compare every claim at low cost.
Exam cue: when a tool can test the whole population cheaply and the aim is to find each exception, choose full-population analysis over sampling.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Due professional care and skepticism. Stakeholders beyond the one who asked
questions.question: Planning assurance on a Ghanaian water utility's collection speed, which its finance director requested, internal auditor Efua learns estimated bills are set high to speed payment. Which view of customers' interests is MOST accurate?

options.A: Relevant: overbilled customers are stakeholders that due care covers
options.B: Not relevant: the finance director is the stakeholder this work serves
options.C: Relevant if billing law limits how estimates may be set
options.D: Not relevant: billing disputes belong to the customer complaints unit

questions.key_concept: Due care weighs the interests of everyone affected by the activity, customers and the public included, not only the person who requested the engagement.
questions.pre_read: Whose interests does due care cover? Look past the person who asked for the work.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 4.2 Due Professional Care requires weighing the interests of those served and of other stakeholders, and its considerations name customers and the public, whose exposure may matter even when it seems unrelated to the organization's goals. Overbilling to speed collection exposes customers whether or not a law is broken, so it belongs in Efua's risk assessment. The legal test, the runner-up, covers only one factor, the probability of noncompliance.

wrong_explanations.B: Due care weighs the interests of those the work is done for, here the finance director, and of other stakeholders too, so overbilled customers count.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: probable noncompliance is one factor of due care. Stakeholders' interests are a separate factor, so overbilling matters even where no billing law applies.
wrong_explanations.D: Handling complaints is management's work, but internal auditors still weigh the risk behind them. Who handles disputes does not decide what the engagement considers.

tips: Eliminate: B, because due care weighs other stakeholders' interests as well as the requester's, and D, because who handles complaints does not decide which risks the engagement weighs.
Final two: A beats C because due care weighs stakeholders' interests as a factor in its own right, beside the separate question of whether any law is broken.
Exam cue: due care looks past the person who asked for the work; customers, staff and the public affected by the activity are part of what the auditor weighs.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Due professional care and skepticism. When strong evidence needs no more
questions.question: Internal auditor Chiara asked a Maltese shipping firm's bank to confirm, directly to Chiara, period-end balances of the three accounts in scope; the reply matches the ledger. Which view of the evidence is MOST accurate?

options.A: Insufficient: treasury's own bank statements are needed to corroborate it
options.B: Sufficient: finance reconciles each of these accounts to the bank monthly
options.C: Insufficient: one source alone cannot support an audit conclusion
options.D: Sufficient: an independent party's reply covers each account tested

questions.key_concept: Skepticism asks how reliable evidence is; information received directly from an independent source is strong, and weaker evidence on top adds nothing.
questions.pre_read: Where did this evidence come from, and how did it reach the auditor? Judge its reliability before asking for more.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 4.3 Professional Skepticism asks how far information can be trusted and calls for more only when something looks incomplete, contradictory or untrue. Standard 14.1 treats information received directly, or from an independent source, as more reliable. The bank's reply came straight to Chiara, covers all three accounts and agrees with the ledger, so it is reliable and sufficient. Statements from treasury, the runner-up, would add a weaker source from the side under review.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: corroboration strengthens doubtful information. This evidence already comes directly from an independent source, and statements passed on by treasury would be weaker, not stronger.
wrong_explanations.B: Monthly reconciliations are management's control, not yet tested here. The confirmation is reliable because it comes directly from an independent party, not because finance reconciles.
wrong_explanations.C: Corroboration is one way to raise reliability, not a rule for every item. A single direct confirmation from an independent source can be sufficient when nothing conflicts with it.

tips: Eliminate: C, because no rule demands two sources for every item, and B, because an untested management control is not what makes this evidence reliable.
Final two: D beats A because skepticism asks how reliable evidence is; a direct, independent reply covering every balance is already strong, and treasury's copies would add a weaker source.
Exam cue: skepticism is not endless checking. Seek more evidence when something might be incomplete or inconsistent; when strong evidence agrees, more weak evidence adds nothing.
